Palestinian tech goes to Silicon Valley

Zackaria Sabella

Kaliza Karuretwa

Karen Grigorian

October 29, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The Palestinian tech delegation in San Francisco. Photo: Oaday Awadalla

This was not a charity evening. It was a business meeting. The room had founders, investors, tech executives, and ecosystem builders from the Silicon Valley and the Arab world.
The event was the centerpiece of a week-long mission organized by the World Bank's Technology for Youth and Jobs project – TechStart – co-financed by the EU, Switzerland, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which brought a Palestinian tech delegation to Silicon Valley in mid-September. The delegation included representatives from the Palestine Techno Park, Ibtikar Fund, the project implementing agency DAI, and nine startups supported by another World Bank initiative, the Innovative Private Sector Development II project – IPSD II. Together, they spent a week meeting with Google, Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon Web Services, Salesforce, Broadcom, and Plug and Play. They also participated in a dedicated panel on the Palestinian tech ecosystem at TechWadi's annual forum, one of the most prominent gatherings of Arab-American tech professionals in the United States.
Across every meeting, the message was clear: these were businesses seeking investment, not sympathy. Palestinian engineers are technically competitive, bilingual, and experienced working with international clients. The cost-quality proposition is strong. Companies supported by TechStart and IPSD II have been delivering for global customers through conditions that would have shut down most startups anywhere else in the world. What Palestinian entrepreneurs need is access: to platforms, to contracts, to the kind of commercial relationships that turn a promising company into a global one. The World Bank’s TechStart and IPSD II projects have together mobilized over $62 million in private capital for the Palestinian tech ecosystem. These are not donor grants, but rather commercial market bets made by investors who see the potential for Palestinian companies to compete and grow in global markets. 
Iyad Zimmo, CEO of Damodi, said the week in San Francisco "put us in the rooms that matter" and helped move investor conversations forward. Hussam Irsheid of PalAID said he arrived focused on growing a local service and left thinking about how to build a global company. For Ibrahim Sana of Farabio, the value was the direct feedback from Silicon Valley practitioners, which helped him see international expansion from a more “practical and actionable” perspective. 
The meetings with major technology companies were candid, thoughtful, and focused on concrete business opportunities. Conversations moved past awareness into practical possibilities: talent pipelines, developer certification, outsourcing pilots, and startup program integration. One global startup support program, open to companies at any stage, had no Palestinian members before the week began. By the end of the meetings, there was shared interest in changing that. The World Bank's role as a trusted intermediary, identifying firms, assessing capabilities, and facilitating introductions, emerged as a clear value proposition that resonated with several counterparts. Some conversations also pointed to the Gulf as an underexplored pathway into global markets through regional investment channels, data centers, and strategic partnerships that could complement the relationships being built in Silicon Valley.
The TechWadi annual forum added another dimension to the week. Representatives from leading venture funds, tech parks, and startups made the case for Palestinian tech to an audience of Arab-American investors and diaspora professionals at the heart of Silicon Valley. What stood out was not the message itself, which was familiar to the panelists, but how it resonated with the audience. Many in the room had not previously viewed the Palestinian tech sector as a commercial destination. By the end of the discussion, they did. A wave of social media posts followed, from people who said the panel changed how they thought about where to invest, where to hire, and where to look for the next generation of technical talent from the Arab world.
None of this turns automatically into contracts or investments. The less visible work begins now: developing pilots and partnerships, connecting startups to global programs, and advancing the investor conversations that started during the week.  Several opportunities are already under discussion, and the World Bank's TechStart and IPSD II are following up on each.
Still, something shifted in San Francisco. Founders walked into rooms where their market was little known and their capabilities were often seen through the lens of crisis. Their sector operates under conditions most ecosystems never face. Yet by the end of the week, the conversations had shifted to business: talent, investment, outsourcing, and global expansion.
Whether pitching in San Francisco or from Ramallah, these entrepreneurs were not seeking validation. They came to challenge perceptions and demonstrate the strength of their businesses. The gap between what the Palestinian technology sector is and what much of the world thinks of it remains significant. But it is narrowing, and the work ahead will determine how fast.
